title: Near-optimal high-rate surgery from linear PCPPs
abstract: A central problem for surgery with quantum Low-Density Parity Check (LDPC) codes is the design of auxiliary systems which measure large sets of logical operators in parallel, while preserving sparsity and fault distance. We introduce a very general method for designing surgery gadgets which are 'high rate', meaning that the number of operators measured in parallel is large in comparison to the size of the auxiliary system. Given an arbitrary initial $[[ n, k, d ]]$ quantum LDPC Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) code, and an arbitrary subcode of size $μ\leq n$ that contains $t \leq k$ logical qubits, the method produces a sparse high-rate surgery gadget with size $μ(\logμ)^{O(\log\log μ)}=μ^{1+o(1)}$ which measures all $t$ logicals in the subcode. The space overhead is asymptotically optimal up to subpolynomial factors, as the lower bound is $Ω(μ)$. This gadget is produced in time polynomial in $μ$. When logical measurement is performed using these surgery gadgets, the phenomenological fault distance is at least $d$ when performed for $d$ rounds.   Our main result comes from relating surgery gadgets with relative cosystolic expansion to linear Probabilistically Checkable Proofs of Proximity (PCPPs), which allow a randomised verifier to probabilistically verify the input to a linear circuit, using only oracle access to the input and a claimed proof.
summary: This paper presents a novel, general method for designing highly efficient auxiliary systems for quantum error correction surgery on LDPC codes. By relating these gadgets to linear Probabilistically Checkable Proofs of Proximity (PCPPs), the authors achieve space overhead that is asymptotically optimal for measuring multiple logical operators. This advances the theoretical understanding of fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_problem: The central challenge is designing sparse, high-rate auxiliary systems for quantum error correction surgery using LDPC codes to measure large sets of logical operators in parallel.
main_result: The authors introduce a general method achieving a space overhead of $\mu^{1+o(1)}$ for measuring $t$ logicals in a subcode of size $\mu$, which is asymptotically optimal.
method: The technique relates the construction of these surgery gadgets to linear Probabilistically Checkable Proofs of Proximity (PCPPs) and utilizes concepts from homological algebra, specifically cochain complexes.
model_or_system: The work analyzes quantum Low-Density Parity Check (LDPC) Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes undergoing 'surgery' operations. The mathematical framework involves constructing and analyzing cochain complexes associated with these codes.
key_observables: Fault distance ($d$), space overhead ($\mu^{1+o(1)}$), and the dimension of homology groups related to logical faults ($ ar{X}$ and $ ar{Z}$ logicals).
important_parameters: Code parameters like blocklength $n$, quantum dimension $k$, and distance $d$; PCPP parameters like randomness complexity $r(n)$ and proof length $\ell(n)$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies heavily on advanced mathematical tools, including the Künneth formula and established theorems regarding linear PCPPs.
figures_summary: Table 1 compares the space, time, and spacetime volume costs of the new method against prior techniques for measuring a subcode.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the physical problem (surgery gadgets) to introducing the mathematical machinery (PCPPs and relative cosystolic expansion) and culminates in proving the near-optimal bounds on the required resources.
why_interesting: The connection between topological/homological methods (cochain complexes) and computational complexity tools (PCPPs) provides a powerful, abstract framework for analyzing resource bounds in quantum error correction.
